inputs.content:
# Parcelbird: should we launch 15-minute grocery delivery? — briefing pack

> **Synthetic benchmark data.** The company, people, competitors and every figure in this pack are fictional. They were generated for a reasoning benchmark and are internally consistent, but they are not real market data.

## 1. Context

Parcelbird, founded in 2023 in Columbus, Ohio, sells software that runs small grocery fulfillment sites (inventory,
picking, rider dispatch) to grocers. ARR is $4.1M, growing 60% a year, gross margin 81%. The company has $12.0M in
cash and burns $0.4M a month.

The founders now propose that Parcelbird become an operator itself: launch **Parcelbird Now**, a 15-minute grocery
delivery service from its own dark stores in Columbus, Indianapolis and Kansas City.

**Decision maker:** the board (two founders and two investors), January 2027.

## 2. Decision question

**Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce grocery delivery service in 2027?**

## 3. Objectives and constraints

- The investors want a path to profitability within the current cash; a new funding round for a delivery
  operator is "unlikely in this market", according to the lead investor.
- Keep at least 12 months of runway at all times.

## 4. The founders' view

"Quick commerce is growing over 40% a year and nobody owns the Midwest. Our software already runs other people's
dark stores, so we know how to run them better than anyone. With density, the unit economics turn positive: our
model shows contribution profit per order by month 18."

## 5. Market

**Table 1. US quick-commerce grocery sales (GMV), $ billions**

| 2022 | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.8 | 2.6 | 3.6 | 5.1 |

**Table 2. Incumbent operators (2025)**

| Operator | Revenue | EBITDA | Contribution per order |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zipcart (national) | $1,200M | −$310M | −$1.90 |
| QuickBasket (regional) | $210M | −$96M | −$3.40 |

QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities in 2025.

## 6. Unit economics

**Table 3. Per-order inputs: industry benchmarks from Parcelbird's software customers (14 sites, 2025) and the founders' plan**

| Input | Benchmark median | Best observed site | Founders' plan |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average order value (AOV) | $34 | $42 | $45 |
| Gross margin on goods | 27% | 27% | 27% |
| Delivery fee collected per order, net of payment cost on it | $1.99 | $1.99 | $1.99 |
| Picking and packing labor per order | $3.10 | $3.10 | $3.10 |
| Rider cost per hour (wage, insurance, vehicle) | $17.75 | $17.75 | $17.75 |
| Orders delivered per rider-hour | 2.4 | 3.0 | 3.5 |
| Dark-store fixed cost per site per year (rent, staff, utilities) | $1.15M | $1.15M | $1.15M |
| Orders per site per day | 900 | 1,400 | 1,800 |
| Payment processing and packaging per order | $1.30 | $1.30 | $1.30 |
| Promotions and discounts, % of AOV | 6% | 6% | 2% |

The best observed AOV and the best observed density are from different sites; no site achieved both. The
benchmark range for orders per rider-hour is 1.9–3.0 and for orders per site per day 400–1,400.

## 7. Columbus pop-up test (six weeks, one temporary site, autumn 2026)

- 11,800 orders; AOV $31; orders grew 18% a week on average.
- Promotions averaged 12% of AOV; riders delivered 2.1 orders per hour; the site averaged 280 orders a day;
  the temporary site's annualised fixed cost was $650,000.

## 8. Customers

- Survey of 1,500 Columbus residents aged 25–39: 44% said they would use 15-minute delivery "at least weekly".
- Pop-up customer data: customer acquisition cost $38 (paid social and first-order credits); 22% of customers
  still ordering in month three; those customers ordered 3.1 times a month.

## 9. Capital

- Founders' plan: 9 dark stores at $0.6M capex each ($5.4M), and a total of $9.5M of cash needed to month 18
  (capex, launch marketing, operating losses), against $12.0M in the bank.

## 10. The software business

- 37 grocers are in the sales pipeline for the software, 9 at the late stage; average contract value $96,000 a year.
- Several grocers in the pipeline want to launch their own fast delivery from existing stores.
- Scaling the software business would need 2 more engineers and 2 sales hires (about $0.8M a year).

## 11. Other material

- **Founders' investor update:** "Zipcart turned contribution-positive in its densest city in Q4 2025 (+$0.40 per
  order). It can be done." Zipcart's shareholder letter adds that this followed a new $3.99 service fee on every
  order and a cut in promotions to 1% of order value, and that order volume in that city fell 14% afterwards.

## 12. Uncertainties

- Whether density in mid-size Midwest cities can reach the benchmark median.
- Whether AOV can rise without losing the convenience use case.
- Rider labor rules: two of the three cities are considering minimum pay standards for delivery workers.

storyline.governing_thought: Parcelbird should not launch Parcelbird Now; it should fund the software business, which nears breakeven within current cash

exec_summary.text: Quick commerce grows fast, but no operator has made it pay

sub_points.text: Zipcart loses $1.90 an order; QuickBasket closed 4 of 11 cities

exec_summary.text: The Columbus pop-up did worse, and few of its customers stayed

Only 22% still ordered in month three, at $173 each to win

exec_summary.text: The software business nears breakeven within current cash

next_steps.action: Decline the Parcelbird Now launch and its $9.5M budget; adopt the four gates
Hire 2 engineers and 2 sales staff for the software business ($0.8M a year)
Close the 9 late-stage grocers and package a fast-delivery offer for grocers' own stores
Report cash against the 12-month runway floor and ARR growth against the 33% gate
Track basket size and rider pace across customer sites against the 3.75-orders gate

constraints.item: Path to profitability within the current $12.0M of cash; new funding for an operator is unlikely
constraints.effect: the recommendation is tested against the current cash only; the software path nears breakeven by end-2028 without new funding

constraints.item: At least 12 months of runway at all times
constraints.effect: the founders' plan leaves about six months at month 18 even in its best case; the software path holds the floor down to 33% growth

constraints.item: Possible minimum pay standards for riders in two of the three cities
constraints.effect: would raise rider cost above $17.75 an hour and widen the per-order loss; each $1 an hour adds about $0.42 an order; carried as gate 4

constraints.item: Customer acquisition and launch marketing not in the unit economics
constraints.effect: per-order contribution excludes $38 acquisition cost; shown separately as $173 per kept customer, and excluded from the pilot cost so that it is a floor

constraints.item: Zipcart's pricing fix cost 14% of volume
constraints.effect: applying the fix to a median site includes the volume loss, which raises site cost per order

alternatives.option: A staged pilot: one permanent Columbus dark store before committing to nine
alternatives.why: it costs about $2.6M in year one, over a third of the cash above the floor, and cannot show the basket and rider pace no customer site has reached; customer-site data is a free test (gate 3)

alternatives.option: Launch, but price like Zipcart (service fee, low promotions)
alternatives.why: a median site still loses about $1.05 an order after site costs once volume falls 14%

failure_threshold.driver: rider pace (orders per rider-hour) for Parcelbird Now; software ARR growth for the recommendation
failure_threshold.threshold: Parcelbird Now covers per-order costs only above 3.75 orders per rider-hour at the median basket, above the best site's 3.0; the software path breaks the runway floor by end-2028 if growth falls below 33% a year with the hires
failure_threshold.range: end-2028 cash on the software path: about $3.2M at 33% growth (low), $3.7M at 40% (stress), $5.4M at 60% (base)

consistency.headline: Parcelbird should not launch Parcelbird Now; it should fund the software business, which nears breakeven within current cash
consistency.fix: worded 'nears breakeven within current cash': the base case reaches about $10.5M of ARR against an $11M breakeven by end-2028, so it does not claim profit by then

gap.target: keep 12 months of runway at all times within the current cash
gap.base_case: the founders' plan leaves $2.5M at month 18 against a $4.8M floor, $2.3M short even in its best case

closers.option: Do not launch; fund the software business with four hires
closers.size: keeps $5.4M at end-2028 at 60% growth and $3.7M at 40%, above the floor

closers.option: Shrink the launch to one site
closers.size: about $2.6M in year one, but proves little

cases.base: software ARR grows 60% a year: about $10.5M at end-2028, $5.4M of cash left
cases.stress: growth of 40% a year: $3.7M of cash at end-2028 against a $2.4M floor

gates.response: hold the second pair of hires and cut other spend

gates.metric: forecast cash against the 12-month runway floor
gates.threshold: under 12 months of burn within two quarters

gates.metric: rider pace at the best customer site
gates.threshold: 3.75 orders per rider-hour held for a quarter at the median basket
gates.response: only then bring a one-site pilot case back to the board

gates.threshold: any rule adopted in Columbus, Indianapolis or Kansas City; each $1 an hour adds about $0.42 an order
gates.response: raise the pace threshold in gate 3
